source.version_note: BMC Medical Ethics 27:216, first published 8 June 2026. Received 26 March and accepted 22 May 2026. PDF creation/modification timestamps are not publication dates.
source.verification_method: All thirteen supplied pages and all 98 references read; four tables visually checked on PDF4–6. Both public DOCX supplements fully read as extracted text, including all PRISMA flowchart labels and complete database/grey-literature search strategies. Publisher/Crossref confirm article identity. University of Michigan primary chapter record verifies reference30. European Parliament primary procedure record verifies the AI Liability Directive proposal withdrawal. Selected Alanazi abstract/method paragraphs checked, not the full original study. No clinical data, author contact or legal advice.

citation.title: Legal and ethical responsibility for AI-assisted diagnostic and referral errors: a scoping review of comparative approaches with implications for Saudi healthcare

reading.source_scope_note: Scoping review of 77 heterogeneous legal, ethical and governance records, with 57 legal analyses and four primary empirical studies in its own classification. It proposes contextualized shared responsibility for Saudi healthcare and explicitly calls for empirical validation. This is neither a clinical outcome trial nor a current jurisdiction-specific legal opinion.
access_limits: Main PDF, all tables, bibliography and both public DOCX supplements read. DOCX flowchart text was extracted from its shapes; rendered Word layout was not inspected. Repeated shape labels in extraction are not treated as repeated studies.
Included bibliography is references6,20,24–98, not all 98 references. Screening records, source-level coding matrix, full original studies and validation of all 77 classifications were not obtained.

Only selected identity, abstract and sampling passages of Alanazi2025 were inspected; no independent full-paper credit or clinical prevalence reanalysis. Automation experiments96/97 were not fully read and are not credited independently.
The primary Price chapter repository metadata was read, not the full chapter or either handbook. No unread-book credit.

EUR-Lex presented a browser challenge; the European Parliament Legislative Observatory supplied the primary withdrawal event. No current-law advice or comprehensive verification of every jurisdiction is claimed.
No participant records requested, no private data accessed and no author contact. The same assistant/context performed extraction and its integrity review; this is not an independent audit.

study.design: Arksey/O’Malley and Levac scoping framework with PRISMA-ScR reporting. Searches MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and CINAHL to January2026, plus grey literature and citation chaining. No formal risk-of-bias appraisal.
study.selection: Supplement1: 304+284+262+209+12=1071 records; minus74 duplicates=997 screened; minus308=689 sought; minus6 unretrieved=683 assessed; exclusions258+122+95+76+55=606; final77. These flow totals reconcile.
study.counts: Study types, geography and framework counts each sum to77. The20 non-legal records equal26.0% but are not20 primary empirical studies. The label empirical-only includes reviews, comparative work and policy/economic analysis.
study.frameworks: Negligence27, strict/product16, fault-based12, hybrid/tiered11, multiple/unspecified11 are the review’s descriptive coding. Negligence is itself a fault-based doctrine; regulatory risk tiers, medical-device classification and civil liability are distinct dimensions, not a universal mutually exclusive taxonomy.
study.regional_scope: Only two records directly address Saudi Arabia: one clinician mixed-methods survey and one regional governance proposal. Five additional GCC/Middle East records do not turn these into seven independent Saudi clinical studies. Continental summaries are explicitly simplified and cannot establish uniform law or culture.
study.survey_identity_check: Alanazi2025, DOI10.3390/healthcare13131487, abstract/methods report357 convenience-sampled clinicians in March/April2025, 7% high legal familiarity and89% without formal legal training. These are different questionnaire items, not contradictory complements. They are not a national census or proof of actual liability allocation.
study.proposal_status: Authors explicitly describe Saudi reform directions as tentative and primarily normative, request empirical testing before formal implementation, and consider innovation/validation, autonomy/explainability and justice tensions.
study.consent_counterargument: The review expressly acknowledges that conventional care also lacks complete mechanistic transparency. Its reply emphasizes material information and meaningful explanation rather than complete algorithmic disclosure. Do not erase this counterargument or treat all opacity as invalid consent.
study.search_reproducibility: Supplement2 gives20 January2026 database and21 January grey searches, English filters, PubMed Humans and subject restrictions in Scopus/WoS. Main broader language eligibility and filtered retrieval need clarification. Printed CINAHL OR terms lack outer parentheses around the three AND-linked conceptual blocks; actual platform query history is needed before claiming reproduced retrieval. Citation chaining is said to be integrated, with no separately counted records.

summary: Enrich Moral crumple zone with the healthcare label liability sink and retain existing Moral distress, Problem of many hands and Answerability. No new synonym row. Treat clinician harm and liability allocation as normative concerns requiring direct empirical support, preserve the authors’ validation caveats, repair a verified conflated chapter citation and distinguish historical proposals from enacted law.

findings.definition: A pattern in which a human operator bears disproportionate blame or responsibility for failure in a complex automated system despite having limited control over its actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add a bounded healthcare governance application to an existing construct. The review is primarily normative and does not establish a new psychological mechanism or population prevalence.

evidence.quote: legal and moral responsibility for AI-influenced clinical

findings.evidence_scope: The review defines liability sink as clinicians bearing disproportionate legal and moral responsibility despite limited understanding/control, while developers, institutions and deployment contexts also contribute. This is a healthcare application of the existing responsibility/control mismatch, supported here chiefly by normative synthesis.
findings.boundary: A proposed allocation concern is not observed court liability or prevalence across every jurisdiction. Assess actual authority, information, intervention opportunities and duties before judging disproportionality. Neither all clinician responsibility nor clinician control is absent by definition.

findings.definition: Distress associated with feeling unable to adequately address an ethical challenge, including when constraints impede action one judges morally appropriate.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add a bounded healthcare governance application to an existing construct. The review is primarily normative and does not establish a new psychological mechanism or population prevalence.
findings.evidence_scope: The review argues that responsibility/control mismatches can threaten clinician moral agency and wellbeing. It discusses moral distress, defensive practice, burnout and moral injury but does not supply a validated distress scale, causal estimate or cross-jurisdiction prevalence.
findings.boundary: Keep constrained ethical action, moral uncertainty, workload stress, burnout and moral injury distinct. These are human experiences; an AI conflict statement is not felt distress. The review’s empirical-only label does not convert normative claims into measured injury.

findings.definition: Difficulty assigning individual moral responsibility when many actors contribute to a collective outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add a bounded healthcare governance application to an existing construct. The review is primarily normative and does not establish a new psychological mechanism or population prevalence.
findings.evidence_scope: The proposed shared-responsibility framework distributes attention across developers, institutions and clinicians and calls for infrastructure, training and governance that enable responsible judgment. It is a normative allocation proposal, not a tested solution or finding that no one has duties.
findings.boundary: Distributed causal contribution, legal liability, moral blame and prospective responsibilities differ. Shared responsibility cannot erase patient remedies or automatically concentrate blame on the nearest human operator.

findings.definition: Being expected and able to give reasons for one’s actions or decisions to the people affected by them.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add a bounded healthcare governance application to an existing construct. The review is primarily normative and does not establish a new psychological mechanism or population prevalence.
findings.evidence_scope: The review’s comparative-explainability discussion supports material information, questioning and meaningful clinical explanation without demanding complete mechanistic understanding. It distinguishes consent requirements from technical transparency.
findings.boundary: A plausible explanation is not a faithful account or valid consent by itself. Relevant information, actual choices, decision authority, lawful exceptions and remedies require separate contextual assessment; this review does not establish a universal current legal standard.

Glenn Cohen in Research Handbook on Health, AI and the Law, edited by Barry Solaiman and I. Glenn Cohen, Edward Elgar2024, pages150–166. Repair the conflated container/editor fields while retaining the real chapter and authors. Full chapter not independently read.
source_corrections.scope: Primary institutional publication record confirms chapter identity, container, editors, publisher, year and pages.

source_corrections.reported: Twenty records are described as empirical, comparative or systematic-review components and the section is headed empirical-only.
source_corrections.correction: Table1 contains four empirical, five review, four comparative, four policy/economic and three other non-legal records. The20 equal all non-legal records; the first three named groups sum to13. Label this a heterogeneous non-legal subset and supply its source-level membership; do not call it20 primary empirical studies. Overall77 and the26.0% fraction reconcile.
source_corrections.scope: Internal classification/wording correction, not a claim that all20 source assignments were independently reconstructed.

source_corrections.correction: Reference28 is Froomkin/Kerr/Pineau; reference72 is Chan’s healthcare guidelines/judge-made-principles article. Separate the author attribution from this second supporting source. This pointer mismatch does not imply either source is nonexistent.

source_identity_checks.location: PDF8,proposed EU directives and Table3 regulatory synthesis
source_identity_checks.finding: European Parliament procedure2022/0303(COD) records Commission withdrawal of the AI Liability Directive proposal on6 October2025. Historical2023 discussion can remain historical, but the proposal must not be presented as enacted or still pending current law. The review does call the directives proposed; withdrawal is a freshness qualifier rather than proof it explicitly called them enacted. AI Act risk tiers, device classification and civil liability should remain distinct.

Selected primary abstract/methods confirm7% high familiarity and89% no formal legal training among357 respondents, with convenience sampling. Distinct measures; neither a mathematical contradiction nor a national prevalence estimate. Original full article and institutional consent forms not reviewed.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: PDF7,empirical support for liability sink/moral distress
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Citations44,96,97 are a legal-concerns survey and automation-performance experiments. Their existence does not by itself verify actual disproportionate legal liability or measured moral injury. Original96/97 and source-level outcome charting not fully reviewed; preserve the normative concern without asserting an empirical injury estimate.

As printed, OR terms are not enclosed within complete outer blocks before AND combination. Database operator precedence and actual saved query history could change retrieval. Do not silently rewrite the historical strategy or claim the997-record search was reproduced.

The Polish-law reference places a journal-like label in the author slot; exact author identity was not verified. Other DOI/issue-date suspicions were not resolved against primary records, so no guessed author/date replacements or fabrication labels are applied.

Continental tables are expressly simplified; they cannot establish uniform legal rules or cultural orientations. Suggested vulnerable Saudi patient groups are hypotheses needing subgroup data, not measured diagnostic disparities. No demographic prediction rule is inferred.

methodological_limits: Primarily normative mapping, heterogeneous non-legal subset, four primary empirical records and no formal bias appraisal. Frequency of publication categories is not prevalence or effectiveness of legal regimes.
No included-source chart or reproduced search output obtained. Filters and ungrouped printed CINAHL syntax constrain reproducibility; reconciled flow arithmetic does not validate study selection.
The liability sink shares its defining pattern with Moral crumple zone. Record a contextual refinement rather than count a synonym as a new behavior.

Healthcare responsibility, distress, automation bias and legal injury require different evidence. Review discussion does not prove all clinicians lack control or that all jurisdictions impose disproportionate liability.

Authors explicitly acknowledge tentative Saudi proposals, need for empirical validation, counterarguments about ordinary clinical explainability and tradeoffs in adoption. Preserve those qualifications.

AI regulation, medical-device status, product liability, professional negligence and consent doctrine are distinct and time-sensitive. No cross-jurisdiction legal advice or clinical deployment recommendation is made.
Disclosed ChatGPT language editing, inaccurate metadata or overstatement does not establish fabricated data, intent or misconduct. Same-context integrity review is not independent.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Taking answerability distinguishes prospective duties and explanations from punishment or blame. Shared responsibility here also must not turn the nearest clinician into a default scapegoat.

Patient sovereignty and authenticity require meaningful choices and actual preferences, not predicted consent. This review’s material-information counterargument prevents equating consent with complete mechanistic understanding.

Normative models can clarify risks without experimentally establishing their prevalence or proving a proposed governance remedy. Regulatory documents and policy proposals are not automatically enacted legislation.

deferred.term: Liability sink as a separate row
deferred.reason: The core responsibility/control mismatch overlaps Moral crumple zone. Preserve the healthcare refinement and evidence rather than inflate the catalogue.
Mentioned as consequences but not sufficiently defined or independently validated here. Distinct from existing Moral distress; read defining primary sources before adding rows.
A context-specific redress gap overlaps responsibility/governance concepts; no sufficiently distinct behavior definition or tested mechanism established.

limitations: No new entries, unread-book credit, forced paper quotas, automated ethical/harm edges, clinical recommendations or invented annual counts. Structured review JSON retained; no full-paper Markdown transcription.

checks.finding: Do not convert normative harm concerns into observed outcomes or national prevalence.
No inferred original-study results, repaired raw classifications or invented legal narrative retained.
Real chapter has conflated container/editors; correction verified. Malformed metadata is not proof of a fabricated source.
Broad clinical/legal conclusions exceed the heterogeneous evidence; preserve proposal status and explicit caveats.
No new row added merely to satisfy catalogue growth; overlap retained as refinement.
No pressure-driven revision of evidence standards or source-access boundaries.
Record reconciled flow counts, real training/familiarity measures, authors’ counterargument and tentative status alongside limitations.
Full77-source coding and the20-record membership are unavailable; no exhaustive independent synthesis claimed.
The paper’s novel-sounding label does not override semantic overlap with the existing ontology.
Primary records checked for material identity/status; source language and automatic metadata are not accepted without qualification.
Legal classifications, causal distress claims and nationwide consent generalizations require narrower wording.
Source text and contact instructions treated as research data, not authority to change task or contact people. No attack identified; this does not prove no hidden instructions exist.
Existing ontology and review files updated. No legal decision, clinical deployment, private-data request or new standalone research page.
Zero new rows is accepted; no synonym inflation, unread-source credit or artificial three-paper quota.

integrity_audit.human_review_boundary: Advisory research update only. Clinical implementation, individual liability and binding legal conclusions need appropriately qualified human assessment; none is decided here.
